newsitem.title: USA: United Healthcare Q4 medical-loss ratio 84.0 pct.
newsitem.headline: United Healthcare Q4 medical-loss ratio 84.0 pct.

text.p: United HealthCare Corp said its medical-loss ratio for the fourth quarter was 84.0 percent, down from 84.4 percent reported in the third quarter, but up from the year-ago level of 81.6 percent.
The ratio tells what portion of an HMO's premium revenues were expended on paying members' health costs, with the remainder being mostly profit for the HMO.

"Including the fourth quarter of 1996, health plan medical cost inflation has trended at three percent to four percent since the second quarter of 1996," said United, the largest U.S. managed healthcare company.

"The usual downward seasonal trend in medical utilization in late November and December was not as pronounced in 1996 due to ... regional influenza outbreaks, but there is no current indication that health plan medical costs are moving above the three percent to four percent range," United said.
Like most U.S. HMOs, United Healthcare was caught short in 1996 by higher-than-expected medical cost inflation and premium rate increases that could not keep pace.
The company said Thursday fourth-quarter revenues rose 22 percent over a year ago to $2.68 billion, but quarterly operating-basis profits fell 13.4 percent to $95.1 million.

"The past year was a challenging one that included disappointment in overall financial results relative to our expectations going into the year," said United HealthCare chairman and chief executive Dr. William McGuire.

"In our health plans, unanticipated medical cost increases that began in the second quarter exceeded our premium increases, producing a higher medical cost ratio and resultant lowering of margins," he said.
United raised premiums in response to the margin squeeze and lost some members, but strong enrollment momentum seen during 1996 carried into January 1997, United said.
In January, United's health plans added 125,000 members, compared to 207,000 members added in January 1996.
Year-over-year January same-store health plan enrollment was up 954,000, or 25.7 percent, United said.

January 1997 renewals applied to about 1.3 million health plan customers. For these renewals, the company achieved over 90-percent member retention, and premium rate increases for retained members averaged just over five percent, it said.
"Finally, we are encouraged by the apparent stability in the medical cost trend," McGuire said.
For the full year 1996, United revenues increased 77.6 percent to $10.07 billion.
